name: Lookism

lead: Lookism means prejudice against people seen as unattractive, or assuming things about someone from how they look. In looksmaxxing it is the reason many men give for working on their looks: people are treated differently based on appearance, so improving yours changes how others respond.

Researchers point to stereotypes that attractive people are more capable or kind, and to employers and others acting on those impressions. Field experiments with fictitious résumés have found callback differences in several countries, and studies report appearance effects on pay and perceived health-care treatment, though size varies by setting.

paras: People use the idea as motivation, picking areas such as grooming, fitness, skin, clothing or height presentation to work on. Forum culture built around the term shares tips and rates progress.

Studies link perceived appearance discrimination with poorer self-rated health, and one analysis of a looksmaxxing forum describes health harms from its appearance-focused norms. Legal protection against appearance discrimination is rare.

chain: Different treatment in hiring and dating
angle.text: Lookism is the term for judging people by appearance, and it is the reason many men give for working on their looks: better presentation changes how people respond in hiring, dating and elsewhere. Sociology and economics research reports real but variable attractiveness effects.

lead: Lookism is prejudice or discrimination against people judged physically unattractive, and more broadly the habit of inferring someone's abilities, character or worth from their appearance. It is studied in sociology, labour economics, psychology, law and bioethics, and it is discussed in hiring, dating, politics, education and healthcare. [1]

In looksmaxxing communities the word is the starting premise: the idea that looks shape how people are treated is the reason given for working on grooming, skin, hair, body composition, dress and, for some, cosmetic procedures. Proponents say that if appearance changes how teachers, employers, friends and partners respond, then improving appearance is a practical way to change those responses. The word was also part of early looksmaxxing forum names, notably Lookism.net. [2][3][4]

Published research reports measurable appearance effects: callback differences in résumé experiments in several countries, wage differences in survey data going back to the 1990s, an association between perceived appearance discrimination and self-rated health, and appearance-linked stereotyping in clinical settings. Researchers disagree about how large these effects are in different jobs and settings, and about whether they amount to injustice. Peer-reviewed work has also begun to study looksmaxxing forums themselves. [1][5][6][7][8]
infobox: Appearance discrimination, beauty bias; the opposite is sometimes called pretty privilege or beauty privilege [1]

paras: Wikipedia describes lookism as prejudice against people considered unattractive, including the judging of intelligence or ability by looks. It can occur in dating, social life and work, and the article notes that it draws less cultural attention and legal protection than racism or sexism. [1]

The concept overlaps with several related terms. The halo effect is a general tendency for an overall impression to colour judgments of specific traits. The physical attractiveness stereotype, often summarised as 'what is beautiful is good', is the specific belief that attractive people are more sociable, successful and moral. Heightism, colorism and weight bias are sometimes treated as particular forms of appearance-based discrimination. Its counterpart, 'pretty privilege', names the advantages said to flow to people seen as attractive. [1][9]

Concern about judging people by appearance is old, and several religious and philosophical traditions warn against it. The word 'lookism' itself gained currency in the 1970s in the fat acceptance movement; a 1978 Washington Post article credited fat people with coining it. [1]

In the 1990s the word moved into university and media vocabulary. Smith College used it to warn incoming students, and columnists such as Joan Beck (1991) argued that the growing list of named prejudices was becoming unwieldy. [1] Psychologist Nancy Etcoff of Massachusetts General Hospital has called lookism one of the most pervasive and least acknowledged prejudices, while also arguing in her book Survival of the Prettiest that attraction has evolutionary roots and that being admired for beauty is not in itself a social harm. [1]

The term halo effect traces to Edward Thorndike's 1920 article on rating errors, in which officers rated soldiers on several qualities and the ratings were highly correlated across traits. [9] In 1972 Dion, Berscheid and Walster showed 60 University of Minnesota students photographs of attractive, average and unattractive people. Participants attributed more socially desirable traits to the attractive people and predicted happier lives and more successful careers and marriages for them. [9]

Later scholars have qualified the idea. Murphy, Jako and Anhalt (1993) argued that some halo effects reflect real correlations between traits rather than rater error, and the stereotype can run the other way, with attractive people sometimes seen as less honest or more conceited. [9] Wikipedia also reports a 1998 study in which newborns only hours old looked longer at attractive faces, which some authors read as evidence of an innate component. [1]

In a 1994 American Economic Review paper, economists Daniel Hamermesh and Jeff Biddle used interviewer ratings of respondents' looks from three surveys, from 1971 to 1981 in the US and Canada. Controlling for demographic and labour-market characteristics, people rated plain earned less than average-looking people, who earned less than those rated good-looking. They estimated the plainness penalty at roughly 5 to 10 percent, somewhat larger than the beauty premium, with slightly larger effects for men than women. [8]

Field experiments sent fictitious résumés with photographs to real job openings. Wikipedia summarises an Argentine study of 2,540 résumés reporting 36 percent more callbacks for attractive applicants, a Peruvian study of 4,899 résumés reporting 82 percent more, and an Israeli study of 5,312 résumés finding an advantage for attractive men but not for women. [1] A 2019 study reported that beauty premiums appear mainly in jobs where looks could affect productivity, such as those with heavy interpersonal contact. [1]

Tietje and Cresap (2005) cited a wage penalty of 7 to 9 percent for the least attractive workers and a premium of about 5 percent for the most attractive third. [1] A survey of 11,000 people from London Guildhall University, reported on Wikipedia, found that people describing themselves as less attractive earned about 13 percent less on average. [10] A 2024 study in Behavioral Sciences examined how a 'lookism climate' and workplace incivility relate to career outcomes among employees. [11]

Studies in Germany, Canada, the US and the UK reported that attractive political candidates tend to win more votes and receive more forgiveness for scandals, with the effect strongest in low-information and candidate-centred elections. [1] One study summarised on Wikipedia found that teachers expected attractive children to be more intelligent and more likely to progress in school. [10]

Height is a frequently cited appearance variable in these discussions. Dan Ariely is reported to have found that American women strongly preferred taller men, and that shorter men needed substantially higher earnings to be judged equally attractive. [1]

A longitudinal study of emerging adults in South Korea reported an association between perceived appearance discrimination and lower self-rated health. [6] A 2024 critical ethnography in Iranian intensive care units described ageism and lookism as stereotypes contributing to health disparities between patients. [7] A 2026 philosophy paper develops the idea of 'aesthetic injustice' in healthcare, in testimonial and hermeneutical forms. [12]
A study of social appearance anxiety found that it mediated the link between Instagram social comparison and acceptance of cosmetic surgery, among workers. [13]

Tietje and Cresap (2005), in a paper titled 'Is Lookism Unjust?', argued that appearance preferences may have biological roots, that looks can be job-relevant when they affect profit, and that remedies would be hard to design. Etcoff has similarly argued that suppressing attraction preferences is neither realistic nor desirable. Others, such as Michelangelo Signorile (1997), compared appearance hierarchies in some communities to racism or sexism, describing 'body fascism' in gay male culture. [1]

Legally, the United States had 'ugly laws' barring people with visible disfigurements from public places until the 1970s. No US federal law prohibits appearance discrimination today, though a few cities do, and the EEOC treats extreme obesity as a disability under the ADA in some circumstances. Belgium's anti-discrimination law of 10 May 2007 covers physical or genetic characteristics. [1]

Wikipedia traces looksmaxxing to manosphere and incel message boards of the 2010s, naming PUAHate.com, Sluthate.com and Lookism.net, sometimes called the PSL forums, as sites where much of the vocabulary, including the PSL rating scale, developed. [3] A lexicographic survey identifies the earliest use of 'looksmaxxing' it knows of in a thread titled 'Looksmaxing' on Lookism.net, dated 29 June 2015, followed by a 4chan post in November 2015 and Reddit posts in 2016. The same source notes that the '-maxxing' suffix predates the word, with a 2013 post using 'bench maxing'. [4] Other sources disagree on exact dates and sites. [3]

The name Lookism.net reflects how the community saw its subject: ranking and discussing appearance as a central social variable. In the 2020s the term looksmaxxing spread to TikTok, where early content was often framed as self-improvement. [3]

subs.h: How the community uses the concept
paras: A 2025 paper in Sociology of Health and Illness analysed 8,072 comments on a looksmaxxing forum reported to have around 6 million unique visitors per month. The authors describe users applying a 'hegemonic masculine gaze' to critique men's faces and bodies, and discuss how the forum's health advice and self-improvement framing can affect men's health. [5]

On looksmax.org, users discuss lookism as lived experience. One thread asks what people do once they are aware of how much looks affect treatment, and another describes frustration over appearance and neurodivergence at work. Posters commonly say that the saying that only inner qualities matter does not match their experience. Other threads describe appearance-related distress in vivid terms, and posters describe wanting to change how they look. [2][14]

Commentators describe lookism as the worldview underneath the blackpill, the belief that women's attraction depends mainly on physical traits and that personality counts for little. [3][15] Researchers reviewing the wider incel phenomenon note appearance-based beliefs as part of its ideology, alongside mental-health burdens. [16]

Jamilla Rosdahl of the Australian College of Applied Psychology wrote in The Conversation in January 2024 that looksmaxxing begins with basic grooming but can progress to steroid use, surgery and bone-breaking, and that it tends to rank men by perceived sexual market value. She argued that broader pressures such as economic insecurity make appearance-focused trends appealing because they offer a sense of control. [17]

Wikipedia notes coverage by Business Insider, The New York Times and the Daily Dot in November 2023, and by The Conversation and the BBC in early 2024. Its looksmaxxing article carries a neutrality-dispute tag, and some of the criticism cited there comes from opinion pieces. [3] Some men report social benefits from the practice, according to the same article. [3]

No clinical trials of lookism itself have been found, since it is a social phenomenon rather than a treatment. Observational and qualitative studies relevant to it include a Korean cohort analysis linking perceived appearance discrimination with self-rated health [6], an ethnography of lookism in intensive care [7], and a study of social appearance anxiety mediating the link between Instagram social comparison and acceptance of cosmetic surgery [13]. Field experiments with fictitious résumés and wage surveys, described above, are the main quantitative evidence on appearance effects in the labour market. [1][8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, lookism is discussed both as a description of how society treats people and as a source of distress, with threads about workplace treatment, neurodiversity and living under appearance pressure. [2][14]

claims.claim: Most people like or dislike you mainly because of your looks.
Being born less attractive makes people worth less to others.
Looksmaxxing forums help men cope with lookism.
Attractive people are assumed to be better people ('what is beautiful is good').
Preference for attractive faces is innate rather than learned.
Being taller or better looking brings higher pay.
Looksmaxxing is a form of self-improvement that can also feed extremist ideas.
